prompt: Which of these sets the CEILING of a log retention policy, rather than its floor?
hint: Personal data cannot be kept beyond its purpose.

choices.text: The size of the disk
choices.why: The disk is a constraint, but the lesson places it last, and it is not a legal limit.

choices.text: The LGPD's principle of necessity
choices.why: Right. It is the reason a policy says when logs are deleted, not only how long they are kept.

choices.text: The twelve months that PCI DSS asks for when a company handles payment cards
choices.why: Also a minimum, set by a contract standard.

choices.text: Article 15 of the Marco Civil da Internet
choices.why: It sets a minimum of six months for application providers: a floor.

prompt: Under article 15 of the Marco Civil da Internet, for how many months does an application provider keep access records?
hint: Half of what a connection provider keeps.

prompt: A company keeps logs for 60 days. A compromise is found in March that began the previous November. What is lost?
hint: Count back from March.

choices.text: The flow records, though the authentication logs survive
choices.why: Both are kept for the same 60 days in this policy.

choices.text: Nothing, since the SIEM keeps alerts for ever
choices.why: Alerts are only as old as the events they were made from, and most events never became alerts.

choices.text: The records of how it started
choices.why: Right. November is outside a 60-day window opened in March.

choices.text: Only the packet captures from March
choices.why: March is inside the window; November is the gap.

prompt: What separates warm storage from hot storage in the lesson's plan?
hint: Both hold logs; the difference is speed and price.

choices.text: Warm is compressed and cheaper, and has to be loaded back before anyone searches it
choices.why: Right. Hot is the SIEM itself, searchable at once and dear per gigabyte.

choices.text: Warm holds only the logs that triggered alerts, because nobody needs to search the quiet ones again
choices.why: It holds the same sources, older.

choices.text: Warm storage is deleted after three months
choices.why: Hot is the three-month tier; warm runs to thirteen.

choices.text: Warm storage keeps the logs unencrypted for speed
choices.why: Encryption is not what separates the tiers.

prompt: What does sending each line to soc as it is written protect against?
hint: Think about what happens to gw on a bad day.

choices.text: Disk space running out on gw, since the lines leave as soon as they are written and nothing piles up
choices.why: The local file on gw grows exactly as before; shipping adds a copy, it does not move the original.

choices.text: Somebody on soc reading the lines without having the permissions that gw would require
choices.why: Permissions on soc are a separate decision, set in the rule.

choices.text: Losing the record together with the machine that wrote it
choices.why: Right. A failed disk or a compromised account on gw no longer reaches the copy on soc.

choices.text: Lines arriving out of order
choices.why: Forwarding adds a second time stamp; it does not reorder anything.

prompt: Without fileCreateMode, fileOwner and fileGroup in the remote rule, the copies on soc came out with mode 644. Why does that matter?
hint: Who can read a 644 file?

choices.text: rsyslog could no longer write to them, so every new line from gw would be dropped silently
choices.why: The owner can write a 644 file.

choices.text: Every user on soc could read logs full of account names and addresses
choices.why: Right. 644 is readable by all; logs with personal data belong to root and adm.

choices.text: logrotate refuses to rotate world-readable files
choices.why: It rotates them; the problem is who reads them.

choices.text: The hash of the file changes with its mode
choices.why: A hash covers the content, not the permissions.

prompt: A line in /var/log/remote/gw.log carries two time stamps minutes apart. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: One stamp is when sshd wrote; the other when rsyslog on gw read and sent.

choices.text: gw and soc are set to different time zones, so the two clocks print different hours for one moment
choices.why: Both are written with their offsets; a zone difference shows as hours, and in the offset.

choices.text: Somebody opened the file on soc and edited the line afterwards by hand
choices.why: An edit would not add a second stamp; the format places both there.

choices.text: soc was unreachable and gw's queue held the lines
choices.why: Right. The queue delays, it does not lose, and the gap shows the outage.

choices.text: ts rounds each stamp to the nearest minute before writing it
choices.why: It writes seconds.

prompt: gw forwards with the template RSYSLOG_SyslogProtocol23Format, which is the message format of RFC ___ and carries the time zone with the time.
hint: The same RFC lesson 1 named for syslog messages.

prompt: `sha256sum -c` prints `FAILED` for a log copy. What does that tell the analyst?
hint: It answers yes or no.

choices.text: Which line of the copy was changed, so the analyst can restore just that one
choices.why: That is what a hash chain adds.

choices.text: Who changed the file
choices.why: A hash knows nothing about people; the custody record does.

choices.text: That the copy differs from the file that was hashed, without saying where
choices.why: Right. A file hash says that something changed; it does not say what.

choices.text: That the disk holding the copy is failing and has started corrupting the files written to it
choices.why: It could be one cause among many; the check does not say.

prompt: Where should the day's hash be kept?
hint: A hash replaced together with its file proves nothing.

choices.text: Apart from the file, where the people who handle the file do not write
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the file and its hash can be replaced together.

choices.text: In the same folder as the file, so that the two are never separated when the file is moved
choices.why: Together, they can be replaced together.

choices.text: Inside the log file, as its last line
choices.why: Adding a line changes the file the hash describes.

choices.text: Nowhere in particular: it can be recomputed from the file at any moment it is needed
choices.why: Recomputing describes the file as it is now, which is the thing in question.

prompt: In the lesson's chain, deleting line 2 left the first hash, f32a8cbd8f4539cc, unchanged. Why?
hint: What does a line's hash cover?

choices.text: sed restored line 1 from a backup it keeps
choices.why: sed -i keeps no backup unless asked.

choices.text: It covers only the start value and line 1, which did not change
choices.why: Right. A link depends on what comes before it, never on what comes after.

choices.text: Hashes are only recomputed for the lines that changed
choices.why: Every hash is recomputed on every run; most simply come out different.

choices.text: The script skips the first line
choices.why: It hashes every line, the first included.

prompt: What does `chattr +a` do to a log file?
hint: a for append.

choices.text: It sends a copy of the file to the remote collector each time a new line is appended
choices.why: That is rsyslog's omfwd.

choices.text: Lines are added, but not rewritten until the attribute is removed
choices.why: Right. Even root has to remove the attribute before rewriting it.

choices.text: It hashes the file every minute
choices.why: It sets an attribute; nothing is hashed.

choices.text: It compresses the file as each line arrives, so that it takes less space on the disk
choices.why: Compression is logrotate's job.

prompt: With `daily` and `rotate 400`, for how many days are old files kept before the oldest is deleted?
hint: One file a day.

prompt: What is the price of `copytruncate` compared with `create` and a signal to rsyslog?
hint: Something happens between two steps.

choices.text: rsyslog has to be restarted every night
choices.why: copytruncate is the option that needs no signal and no restart.

choices.text: The rotated file cannot be compressed
choices.why: It can; compress applies either way.

choices.text: A line written between the copy and the truncation is lost
choices.why: Right. The writer keeps its file open, and that brief window is the cost.

choices.text: The old file loses its owner and group
choices.why: The listing shows syslog and adm on both files.

prompt: Why does the lesson's configuration use `dateext`?
hint: Compare gw.log-20261007 with gw.log.1.

choices.text: Because logrotate refuses to compress numbered files
choices.why: It compresses both kinds.

choices.text: So that rsyslog starts writing the full date into each line it receives from now on
choices.why: Lines carry their own time stamps already.

choices.text: To keep the rotated file in the hot tier, where the SIEM can still search it directly
choices.why: Tiers are about where files live, not their names.

choices.text: So a name says which day it holds
choices.why: Right. A numbered file shifts every night; a dated one does not.

prompt: Which Brazilian text defines the chain of custody stage by stage, for evidence in criminal proceedings?
hint: Articles 158-A to 158-F.

choices.text: The Code of Criminal Procedure, as changed by Law 13.964/2019
choices.why: Right. Articles 158-A to 158-F, from recognising evidence to discarding it.

choices.text: The Marco Civil da Internet
choices.why: It sets retention periods for providers.

choices.text: ISO/IEC 27037
choices.why: An international guideline, not Brazilian law.

choices.text: The LGPD
choices.why: The LGPD governs personal data; custody of evidence is procedural law.

prompt: An analyst wants to search the collected log. What does the lesson say to do first?
hint: The collected file stays untouched.

choices.text: Open the collected file read-only and search it there
choices.why: Read-only access still risks the original; the rule is to work on copies.

choices.text: Note the transfer at the end of the week
choices.why: Transfers are recorded when they happen.

choices.text: Compress it first, so that it cannot be edited by accident while being searched
choices.why: Compression changes the file and its hash.

choices.text: Make a copy and check its hash against the record
choices.why: Right. Work on copies, and confirm each one matches before trusting it.

prompt: Match each technique to the question it answers.
hint: Availability, change, place of change, people.

pairs.right: is there still a copy if gw is lost?

pairs.left: a SHA-256 of the day's file
pairs.right: is this the file that was collected?
from which line on did it change?

prompt: Order the life of one day's log on soc, from first line to last record.
hint: It is written, closed, sealed, then handed over.
items: lines arrive from gw over TCP
logrotate closes the day as gw.log-20261007
the analyst hashes the closed file and stores the hash apart
a transfer to the investigator is written in the custody record

prompt: A colleague hands you a log and its SHA-256 on the same USB stick, and the hash matches. What can you conclude?
hint: What would a swap of both look like?

choices.text: That the log is the one collected, since SHA-256 cannot be forged
choices.why: Nobody forged the hash; it could simply have been recomputed over a changed file.

choices.text: Only that file and hash agree; both could have been swapped together
choices.why: Right. The hash needs a custody record, and a copy kept apart, to mean more.

choices.text: That the log is complete and in order, with no line missing from the day it covers
choices.why: A matching hash says the file is the one hashed, not that nothing was missing then.

choices.text: Nothing: hashes on USB sticks are invalid
choices.why: The medium does not matter; who could change it does.
